claims.claim: Emotion is rendered as bodily sensation through concrete simile.
claims.quote: Fear filled his gut like a meal he could not digest

claims.claim: Sword-clash is described by an unexpected animal comparison instead of the stock metallic one.
claims.quote: like an animal screaming in pain

claims.claim: Characters are introduced by paired antitheses against a sibling.
claims.quote: slender where Robb was muscular, dark where Robb was fair

claims.claim: Important moments are slowed and packed with concrete specifics rather than rushed.
Backstory enters when a remark prompts the POV character's memory rather than by narrator summary.
claims.source: Dark Jackel's Howl, 'Let's Read AGOT Part 1', 2015-08-19
claims.quote: some character makes a comment or observation, which prompts memories

claims.claim: The prologue builds dread through negative sensory statements and dialogue with double meanings.
claims.source: The Fantasy Review, 'Prologue Summary and Analysis', 2023-10-14

claims.claim: Battle description opens ornate and tips into graphic gore, with spatial confusion left intentional.
claims.source: Race for the Iron Throne (Steven Attewell), Tyrion VIII, 2014-01-30

claims.claim: Earlier physical detail (Bran's gargoyle handholds) is re-used as an instrument of later violence.
claims.source: Race for the Iron Throne (Steven Attewell), Bran VII ACOK, 2016-04-07
claims.quote: His tongue felt strange and thick in his mouth

claims.claim: A repeated phrase in a doomed POV ('the bloody snow') carries foreshadowing the character cannot read.
claims.source: Race for the Iron Throne (Steven Attewell), ASOS Prologue, 2016-04-18

claims.claim: Fan close readers note full names in narration assert agency while 'the dwarf' appears ten times in one depressed Tyrion chapter.
Jaime's italic commentary goes silent immediately before a violent act, forcing the reader to register it.
'Nuncle' and similar archaisms (pease, neeps) appear only from A Feast for Crows onward, a deliberate late shift some readers dislike.
claims.quote: It's totally an AFFC and onward thing

claims.claim: A phrase like 'Only the cold' recurs across Jon's death-adjacent moments to bind them.
Reading-group posters contrast Martin's crisp, fast, gritty prose with Kay's slow lyricism, while one flags excessive wordiness.
claims.source: Goodreads Sword & Laser thread, 'Kay or Martin?'
claims.quote: fast where Kay is slow; gritty where Kay is lyrical

claims.claim: Each chapter is named for its POV and the reader knows only what that character knows, who may be an unreliable witness.
claims.quote: the reader only knows what the main character knows

verdicts.trueWording: "Fear filled his gut like a meal he could not digest."
verdicts.note: Appears word for word under the post's "Ingredient # 1: Direct POV character experience of dread and fear". The page does not itself use the words 'bodily sensation' or 'simile', but quotes the line as its example of POV-rendered fear.

verdicts.trueWording: "only a high, thin sound at the edge of hearing, like an animal screaming in pain"
verdicts.note: Word for word, and the claim's contrast is explicit on the page: "there was no ring of metal on metal". The post labels it 'defamiliarized' and explains the technique.

verdicts.trueWording: "Jon was slender where Robb was muscular, dark where Robb was fair, graceful and quick where his half brother was strong and fast."
verdicts.note: The quoted fragment is an exact substring. Page frames it as "a comparative version of the familiar 'three stroke' rule of character creation"; Robb is named as the half brother, so 'against a sibling' holds.

No quote supplied, and none needed: page says "Martin doesn't rush the execution scene - quite the contrary. Time slows down. There's an abundance of detail". It credits the term 'crowding' to Ursula K. Leguin, which the claim omits.

verdicts.trueWording: "some character makes a comment or observation, which prompts memories and reactions from the POV character, Will"
verdicts.note: Exact substring. 'rather than by narrator summary' is the claim's gloss on the page's "it's pretty minimalist" framing of the expositional style.

Word for word, but as the post's epigraph excerpt from the novel (with "The woods gave no answer"), not as the blogger's own analysis. The 'double meanings' half IS the page's analysis: the opening exchange is "clever wordplay" that on reread is "telling you to be very, very afraid of the dead". The page never uses the phrase 'negative sensory statements'.

verdicts.trueWording: "the likening of the Lannister host to an 'iron rose, thorns gleaming' is typical"
verdicts.note: Exact. Page: "Martin's prose is almost lyrical... From there though, the narrative soon descends into the blood and gore". The intentional-confusion half is also explicit: "I think the confusion is intentional for several reasons", about mistaking an east-west for a north-south orientation.

verdicts.trueWording: "the gargoyles that were Bran's handholds transformed into murder weapons"
verdicts.note: The supplied quote "His tongue felt strange and thick in his mouth" IS on the page word for word, but it is a block quote about Bran's warging and does NOT evidence this claim. The claim's actual support is the separate sentence given as trueWording, which the claim calls "deliberate and thorough" callback. Quote/claim are mispaired.

verdicts.trueWording: "GRRM loves a cheap pun, Chett's downfall is caused by snow"
verdicts.note: The doomed-POV foreshadowing the character cannot read is supported. But 'refrain' overstates: the page carries "the bloody snow" once as its epigraph and once inside the quoted Chett passage; it never calls it a repeated phrase or refrain.

verdicts.trueWording: "every sentence is a declaration of Tyrion's will"
verdicts.note: Both halves check out. The count is near-verbatim on the page: "'the dwarf' as a descriptor appears ten times in the narrative in Tyrion's first chapter in ADWD alone, at a time where his headspace is full of depression and self-loathing". Claim supplied no quote, hence SUBSTANCE not VERBATIM.

verdicts.trueWording: "jaime's smart-mouthed inner voice is absolutely SILENT about his feelings about brienne"
verdicts.note: Exact, capitalisation included. 'forcing the reader to register it' is supported: "he wants that jolt, he wants to shake you. he wants you to NOTICE." Caveat: the page says 'inner voice'/'inner commentary'/'inner snarkbot', never 'italic'; and the silence runs through the Ronnet Connington exchange, with Jaime's golden hand striking him at the end.

verdicts.trueWording: "But it's totally an AFFC and onward thing, with GRRM deliberately archaic-ing his language (to many people's annoyance)"
verdicts.note: Exact substring, and the dislike is the blogger's own (tag: "i am not a great fan of the archaic-ing of asoiaf"). Caveat: only 'nuncle' is dated to AFFC-onward. 'pease' and 'neeps' appear in a different post as "Other GRRM-style words from archaic English" with no book range attached, so the claim's parenthetical extends the source.

The string "Only the cold..." appears exactly once on the page, inside a block quote of Jon's last ADWD chapter. The page's point is a cross-POV pairing - Sixskins' death ("a shock of cold") against Jon's - not a phrase recurring across Jon's own death-adjacent moments. No refrain or recurrence is claimed anywhere on the page. Note also the URL is the blog homepage, whose contents rotate; the relevant post is 'Jon's death: On further thinking...', 2015-08-03.

verdicts.trueWording: "He's fast where Kay is slow; gritty where Kay is lyrical; despairing where Kay is poignant."
verdicts.note: Exact substring (poster Kam, msg 40). Every element checks: 'HD' is msg 2, "Martin seems to write in HD, where Kay uses a soft filter at times" plus "Martin's pacing and action are crisper"; the wordiness flag is msg 6, "can be given over to excessive wordiness, but his action is incomparable".

verdicts.trueWording: "With a limited point of view, the reader only knows what the main character knows."
verdicts.note: Exact substring. Both other elements are explicit: "the POV character gets his or her chapter named after them" and "he or she could be an unreliable witness".
